notes.title: Propositions and truth values
Truth tables, computed by enumeration
De Morgan's laws, verified by brute force
Implication and the contrapositive
Predicate logic over finite domains
notes.body: Predicates add quantifiers: `FORALL x, P(x)` and `EXISTS x, P(x)`. Over a finite domain you can evaluate them by enumeration. Worked example: domain = {2, 3, 4}, statement `EXISTS x, x is prime AND x > 3`. Check: x=2 (prime, not >3, fails), x=3 (prime, not >3, fails), x=4 (not prime, fails). No witness exists, so the statement is **false**. Change `>3` to `>=3`: x=3 is prime and >= 3, so the statement becomes **true**. Existence claims need exactly one witness; universal claims need every case. This discipline maps directly onto testing: 'there exists an input that crashes' vs 'for all inputs it terminates'.

notes.title: Boolean algebra for systems work
notes.body: Boolean algebra gives simplification laws: absorption `p OR (p AND q) = p`, distribution, idempotence `p AND p = p`. Worked example: simplify `(admin AND active) OR (admin AND NOT active)`. Factor admin: `admin AND (active OR NOT active)` = `admin AND T` = **admin**. Verified by enumerating all 4 assignments of (admin, active): both sides agree on every row. Why it matters: access-policy engines evaluate exactly these expressions. Simplifying before deploying means fewer rules, faster evaluation, and policies a human can audit. Detection rules are logical expressions over events; write them precisely.

notes.body: E[X] = Σ x·P(x): the long-run average. Worked example: a retry policy succeeds on attempt 1 with p=0.7, attempt 2 with p=0.2, attempt 3 with p=0.1 (then gives up). Expected attempts = 1×0.7 + 2×0.2 + 3×0.1 = **1.4000000000000001**. Linearity of expectation: E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even when X,Y are dependent — the workhorse for analyzing total cost, total latency, total errors across components without modeling their joint distribution.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: - **bash for operations** — the shell as an operations platform: looping over targets, parsing command output at speed. - **text processing pipeline** — grep, sed, awk, cut, sort, and uniq chained over scan output; the attacker’s spreadsheet. - **SUID** — the set-user-ID permission bit: a binary that runs as its owner; the classic Linux privilege-escalation surface. - **persistence mechanism** — cron jobs and services, the footholds that survive reboots; you learn them to recognize them. - **TCP/IP for attackers** — reading what each header field leaks: TTL and window sizes hint the OS, sequence numbers hint the stack. - **host discovery** — finding which hosts are alive before you scan a single port; recon’s first question. - **connect scan** — a full TCP handshake per port; loud, reliable, and logged everywhere. - **SYN scan** — the half-open scan; quieter than a connect scan, and the attacker’s default. - **UDP scan** — slow and unreliable, but UDP services hide some of the best vulnerabilities. - **vulnerability scanning** — service detection plus version fingerprinting: identify the software, pin the exact version, match the known weakness. - **exploitation workflow** — recon → scan → exploit → post-exploitation; the grammar every attack in this course follows. - **passive reconnaissance** — DNS, WHOIS, certificate transparency, breach data, social media; zero contact with the target. - **active reconnaissance** — anything that touches the target; it announces you and requires authorization. - **OSINT tradecraft** — sock puppets and compartmentation; operational security for the investigator. - **documentation discipline** — every finding sourced and timestamped; the lab report starts at recon, not at the shell. - **hash identification** — recognizing the hash format first (hash-identifier thinking) so the attack matches the algorithm. - **rule-based cracking** — a wordlist plus mangling rules — leetspeak substitutions, ?d?d?d?d appends — multiplies a list roughly 100x; attackers think in rules, not bigger lists. - **keyspace** — the total number of candidate passwords; time-to-crack is keyspace divided by hashrate. - **credential hygiene** — the defender’s lesson from cracking: length, uniqueness, and MFA beat every clever password. - **802.11 fundamentals** — how Wi-Fi frames, beacons, and authentication actually work; the prerequisite to attacking or defending wireless. - **4-way handshake** — the WPA2 key exchange; capture it and the crack happens offline, at your speed. - **deauthentication attack** — forcing a client to reconnect so you can capture its handshake; on your own lab network only. - **WPA3** — the current Wi-Fi standard; resists the offline dictionary attacks that fell WPA2. - **PMF** — Protected Management Frames; the defense that defeats deauthentication attacks. - **rogue-AP detection** — finding evil-twin access points impersonating your network. - **Burp methodology** — proxy to observe, repeater to manipulate by hand, intruder to automate, decoder to transform; methodology before automation. - **injection flaw** — SQL injection, command injection, cross-site scripting; untrusted input reaching an interpreter is the vulnerability. - **attack surface** — in web exploitation, every input field, header, and parameter is the attack surface. - **authentication attack** — brute force, session-handling abuse, MFA bypass shapes; identity is the perimeter now. - **disk forensics** — file carving, deleted-file recovery, registry and USN analysis; the artifacts your attack leaves behind. - **memory forensics** — process lists, injected code, network connections; memory is where malware lives. - **super-timeline** — filesystem, registry, and log events merged into one chronological view of the intrusion. - **anti-forensics** — timestomping, log wiping; you learn it so you can detect it. - **Modbus** — the OT protocol with no authentication by design; you don’t patch it, you segment around it. - **DNP3** — the utility-sector control protocol; the same unauthenticated heritage as Modbus. - **air-gapped lab** — the only acceptable OT practice environment: no route to production, ever. - **safety-critical ethics** — OT attacks can kill people; that fact outranks every technique in this module. - **NICE Framework** — the workforce taxonomy this spine maps to: OG (Oversight/Governance), DD (Design/Development), IO (Implementation/Operation), PD (Protection/Defense), IN (Investigation).

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: - **machine methodology** — recon → enumerate → exploit → privilege-escalate → loot → report; the loop you run on every lab box. - **enumeration discipline** — every port, every service, every version; the vulnerability hides in the boring service you skipped. - **Linux privesc patterns** — SUID binaries, cron jobs, writable PATH and service files, kernel version, sudo rights; the checklist you run on every shell. - **Windows privesc patterns** — unquoted service paths, weak service permissions, AlwaysInstallElevated, token privileges; the Windows twin of the Linux checklist. - **‘try harder’, correctly understood** — enumerate more, not guess more; the PEN-200 methodology in three words. - **buffer overflow** — the rite of passage: fuzz to crash, find the offset, control EIP, deliver shellcode; it teaches the stack disguised as an exploit. - **EIP control** — overwriting the instruction pointer; the moment a crash becomes an exploit. - **DEP/ASLR** — Data Execution Prevention and Address Space Layout Randomization; the mitigations that make classic overflows a fundamentals lesson. - **SQLi→RCE** — turning SQL injection into remote code execution: xp_cmdshell, writing web shells; the web chain that ends in a shell. - **SSRF** — server-side request forgery: making the server fetch a URL you chose; the pivot from web bug to infrastructure access. - **cloud metadata service** — 169.254.169.254: instance credentials over HTTP; the SSRF crown jewel and the keys to the kingdom. - **IMDSv2 defense** — hop limits and token requirements that blunt SSRF-to-metadata attacks; know the defense with the attack. - **deserialization** — untrusted object graphs decoded into live objects; gadget chains turn it into remote code execution. - **race condition (TOCTOU)** — time-of-check to time-of-use: the timing attack that wins when two operations interleave wrong. - **Kerberoasting** — requesting crackable (RC4) service tickets as any domain user, then cracking them offline; the service account’s password, no privileges required. - **AS-REP roasting** — accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled let you request the AS-REP directly and crack it offline. - **BloodHound thinking** — attack the graph, not the host: find the shortest path to Domain Admin through misconfigurations first, exploit second. - **lateral movement** — PSExec, WMI, WinRM, pass-the-hash; moving through the network with captured credentials. - **pass-the-hash** — authenticating with the hash itself, no cracking required; why hashes are password-equivalent. - **Golden Ticket** — a forged Kerberos ticket-granting ticket; domain dominance that betrays itself in ticket metadata. - **DCSync** — replicating directory secrets like a domain controller; detected in event 4662 replication anomalies. - **event 4769** — the Kerberos service-ticket request log; anomalies here are the Kerberoasting detection. - **T0–T3 CTF architecture** — T0 guided warmups, T1 single-technique, T2 chained scenarios, T3 research-grade original problems. - **finding write-up** — title, severity, CVSS, evidence, business impact, remediation, retest; the anatomy of a finding that gets fixed. - **risk rating** — likelihood times impact, stated honestly; inflating severity burns credibility at retest. - **executive summary** — the one page the board actually reads; findings are for engineers, summaries are for decisions. - **retest verification** — proving the fix worked; the step where client trust compounds.

Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Security work punishes cowboy habits. In Offensive Operations: HTB, THM, OffSec, internalize these:
- **Tool-first thinking.** Running the scanner before forming a hypothesis. Methodology first: enumerate, hypothesize, test, document — tools serve the method, not the reverse.
- **Scope drift.** Touching anything outside written authorization, even 'just to check.' Scope is a legal boundary, not a suggestion.
- **Findings without evidence.** A claim with no timestamp, screenshot, log line, or packet capture is a rumor. Capture evidence as you go; you cannot reconstruct it later.
- **Alert fatigue.** Tuning out noisy detections trains you to miss the real one. Fix the noise at the source instead of training yourself to ignore it.
- **Lab-equals-enterprise fallacy.** Your lab's flat network and single domain are not the target environment. Note every assumption that won't survive contact with production.
- **Skipping the report.** The assessment isn't done when the testing stops — it's done when someone can act on the writeup. Findings need impact, evidence, and remediation.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: - **L1 triage** — alert to quick classification: true or false positive, severity, escalate or close; speed with accuracy, measured by time-to-triage. - **L2 investigation** — pulling the logs, building the timeline, correlating across EDR, firewall, proxy, and identity; depth after the L1 handoff. - **L3 threat hunting** — hypothesis-driven searches (‘what would this adversary do here?’); hunts that find things become detections. - **detection engineering** — the discipline of turning hunts into deployed, tuned detections; the bridge between red knowledge and blue operations. - **Sigma** — the open detection format: title, logsource, detection (selection plus filter plus condition), level; write once, convert to Splunk, Elastic, or Sentinel. - **logsource** — the Sigma field naming what the rule watches; a rule is only as good as its log source’s coverage. - **false positive tuning** — baseline, threshold, allowlist; false positives are the tax on detection, budgeted and tuned — never silently tolerated. - **blind spot** — what a log source cannot tell you; blind spots drive the logging roadmap, because you can’t detect what you don’t log. - **disk forensics** — file carving, deleted-file recovery, registry and USN analysis; the persistent record of the intrusion. - **memory forensics** — process lists, injected code, network connections; memory is where malware lives — and it evaporates. - **network forensics** — PCAP timelines and C2 beacons: regular intervals plus consistent sizes are the beacon pattern. - **order of volatility** — memory before disk, always; collect the ephemeral first in live response. - **IR lifecycle** — preparation → detection and analysis → containment → eradication → recovery → lessons learned; the exam and the job agree on this order. - **short-term containment** — isolate the host now; stop the bleeding before you diagnose. - **long-term containment** — rebuild and harden; the fix that survives the attacker’s return. - **chain of custody** — hash everything (SHA-256) and document every hand; evidence that survives challenge. - **super-timeline** — log2timeline-style merged timelines; the story of the intrusion in one view. - **threat-informed defense** — mapping detections to MITRE ATT&CK; coverage gaps become the hunting backlog, and vague ‘better detection’ becomes a shopping list. - **impossible travel** — same identity, two distant locations, minutes apart; paired with a fresh MFA enrollment it’s the account-takeover pattern. - **JA3** — the TLS client fingerprint; odd JA3 plus beaconing intervals confirms C2 in PCAP. - **blameless postmortem** — fix the system, not the person; blame hides the next incident. - **lessons learned** — the IR report that prevents recurrence; an incident response without it is just firefighting. - **Security+ bridge** — the SY0-701 defensive vocabulary and readiness gate in this module; full preparation lives in IL-09.

notes.title: Worked example: Phishing wave hits M365. Sentinel workflow?
Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Security work punishes cowboy habits. In Security Operations on Microsoft Sentinel: SC-200, internalize these:
- **Tool-first thinking.** Running the scanner before forming a hypothesis. Methodology first: enumerate, hypothesize, test, document — tools serve the method, not the reverse.
- **Scope drift.** Touching anything outside written authorization, even 'just to check.' Scope is a legal boundary, not a suggestion.
- **Findings without evidence.** A claim with no timestamp, screenshot, log line, or packet capture is a rumor. Capture evidence as you go; you cannot reconstruct it later.
- **Alert fatigue.** Tuning out noisy detections trains you to miss the real one. Fix the noise at the source instead of training yourself to ignore it.
- **Lab-equals-enterprise fallacy.** Your lab's flat network and single domain are not the target environment. Note every assumption that won't survive contact with production.
- **Skipping the report.** The assessment isn't done when the testing stops — it's done when someone can act on the writeup. Findings need impact, evidence, and remediation.

scriptLabs.title: Recon Pipeline: Passive-First Scripting
scriptLabs.brief: Build a passive recon script: given a domain, pull certificate transparency (crt.sh), DNS records, and WHOIS — no packets to the target. Required fragments enforce the passive discipline.
scriptLabs.starter:

"""Passive recon: crt.sh + DNS + WHOIS. No active scanning."""
import json, subprocess, sys, urllib.request

domain = sys.argv[1]
# TODO 1: crt.sh JSON for subdomains
# TODO 2: DNS records via dig (A, MX, TXT)
# TODO 3: WHOIS registrar + dates
# print a findings report

scriptLabs.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Passive recon: crt.sh + DNS + WHOIS. No active scanning."""
import json, subprocess, sys, urllib.request

domain = sys.argv[1]
print(f'=== passive recon: {domain} ===')

# 1. Certificate transparency: subdomains from public logs (fully passive)
url = f'https://crt.sh/?q=%.{domain}&output=json'
try:
    data = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=30))
    subs = sorted({e['name_value'] for e in data})
    print(f'--- crt.sh: {len(subs)} names ---')
    print('\n'.join(subs[:50]))
except Exception as ex:
    print('crt.sh failed:', ex)

# 2. DNS via the resolver (not the target)
for rtype in ('A', 'MX', 'TXT', 'NS'):
    out = subprocess.run(['dig', '+short', domain, rtype], capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(f'--- DNS {rtype} ---\n{out.stdout.strip() or "(none)"}')

# 3. WHOIS: registrar and dates
out = subprocess.run(['whois', domain], capture_output=True, text=True)
for line in out.stdout.splitlines():
    if any(k in line.lower() for k in ('registrar:', 'creation date', 'expiry')):
        print('WHOIS:', line.strip())
print('=== done: zero packets to target ports ===')

title: Suspicious PowerShell Encoded Command
id: 11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555
status: test
description: Detects PowerShell with -EncodedCommand or download cradles (IEX/DownloadString) - common attacker tradecraft.
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-EncodedCommand'
      - '-enc '
      - 'IEX'
      - 'DownloadString'
      - 'Invoke-Mimikatz'
  filter_admin:

  condition: selection and not filter_admin
falsepositives:
  - Admin automation using encoded commands
  - Software deployment tools
level: high

scriptLabs.title: KQL Hunt: Impossible Travel
scriptLabs.brief: Write a KQL query finding impossible-travel logons: same user, two distant locations, within 60 minutes. Required fragments force the self-join pattern.
scriptLabs.starter:
// TODO: SigninLogs, two logons same user, different cities, < 60 min apart
// HINT: join the table to itself on UserPrincipalName, filter time delta and location difference
scriptLabs.hint: A=SigninLogs | where ResultType==0; B=A; A | join kind=inner (UserPrincipalName) B | where A.TimeGenerated < B.TimeGenerated and datetime_diff('minute', A.TimeGenerated, B.TimeGenerated) between (1..60) and A.LocationDetails.city != B.LocationDetails.city
scriptLabs.solution:
let window = 60; // minutes
SigninLogs
| where ResultType == 0  // successful logons only
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, City = LocationDetails.city, IPAddress
| join kind=inner (
    SigninLogs
    | where ResultType == 0
    | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, City = LocationDetails.city, IPAddress
  ) on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated < TimeGenerated1
| where datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, TimeGenerated1) between (1 .. window)
| where City != City1
| project UserPrincipalName, FirstCity=City, FirstTime=TimeGenerated, SecondCity=City1, SecondTime=TimeGenerated1,
    MinutesApart=datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, TimeGenerated1)
| order by MinutesApart asc
// Tune: allowlist VPN egress cities; alert on <30 min intercontinental pairs first.

blocks.body: Passive → active recon → enumerate deeply (70%) → exploit → privesc (SUID/cron/paths) → loot → document from minute one
Kerberoasting (4769) · AS-REP roast (no pre-auth) · BloodHound shortest path · lateral (PSExec/WMI) · Golden Ticket/DCSync = domain dominance
Burp: proxy→repeater→intruder · SQLi→RCE · SSRF→169.254.169.254 (IMDSv2 defends) · deserialization = RCE · race = TOCTOU
Legal targets only · documented authorization · stay in scope · report with remediation · responsible disclosure
L1 triage (speed) → L2 correlate (depth) → L3 hunt (hypotheses) · contain before eradicate · memory before disk
Sigma: title/logsource/detection/level · hunts become rules · tune FPs, don't tolerate · ATT&CK maps the gaps
Prepare → detect → contain → eradicate → recover → lessons-learned · chain of custody: hash + document · blameless postmortems
Hypothesis first · join for impossible travel · connectors before rules · playbooks: enrich→act · filter ingestion at source
Passive first: DNS, certs, WHOIS, GitHub, Shodan. Active: ping sweep → port scan (nmap) → service/version fingerprint → vuln mapping. Scope in writing before a single packet.
Match service versions to CVEs; prefer misconfiguration over 0-days. One shell is worth ten theories — but screenshot everything for the report.
Linux: sudo -l, SUID binaries, cron jobs, kernel version. Windows: unquoted service paths, AlwaysInstallElevated, token impersonation, AD misconfig.
Kerberoasting (crackable SPN tickets) → AS-REP roasting (no pre-auth) → DCSync (replication rights) → Golden Ticket (krbtgt hash). BloodHound maps the shortest path.
Finding = evidence + impact + likelihood + remediation + retest steps. Executive summary in business risk, appendix in packet detail.
1) What fired and why (rule logic). 2) Asset criticality. 3) Corroboration (2+ independent signals). 4) Disposition: true/false positive, benign-true, or escalate.
Severity = confidence × asset value × blast radius. A certain alert on a DC outranks a maybe on a kiosk.
Isolate host (EDR), disable account, block IOC at firewall/proxy — in that order. Preserve volatile evidence (memory, logs) before reimaging.
Every detection needs: hypothesis (ATT&CK technique), data source, logic, tuning baseline, and a runbook. Detections without runbooks are noise.

Threat capability × vulnerability exploitability × business impact. Fix the product of the three, not each in isolation.

answerBank.q: How do I start in cybersecurity with no background?
answerBank.a: The spine: Linux + networking + the Security+ bridge (Module 1 + Module 3's gate), then pick red or blue. Labs on legal targets from day one — reading without doing doesn't transfer in security.

As a methodology credential, yes — it's the most respected hands-on cert in pentesting. Budget 3-6 months of lab time. This module maps PEN-200's methodology; the exam itself is OffSec's 24-hour practical.
Learn both basics, then follow the work you can't stop doing: hunters love the chase (blue), breakers love the puzzle (red). The market needs both; the module trains both so you choose informed.

answerBank.q: Is AI going to replace SOC analysts?
answerBank.a: No — it amplifies them. AI drafts summaries and queries; analysts verify, decide, and handle the novel. The module's AI discipline (verify before action) is the skill that keeps you employed.
Possible but painful — get AZ-900-level Azure familiarity first, then the module's KQL depth. The exam is 40%+ environment/ATT&CK mapping; portal fluency matters as much as query skill.

answerBank.q: What's the single highest-value defensive skill?
answerBank.a: Detection engineering: turning hunts into Sigma rules tuned to your environment. It's the bridge between red knowledge and blue operations — and it's chronically understaffed.

glossary.definition: Authorized simulated attack, scoped in writing: recon → exploitation → privilege escalation → reporting.
Information gathering before attack: passive (OSINT) then active (scanning). The phase that determines everything after.
Moving from low-privilege access to SYSTEM/root/admin via misconfigurations or vulnerabilities.
Spreading from the initial foothold to other hosts, usually toward high-value targets like domain controllers.
Requesting crackable Kerberos service tickets for SPN accounts and brute-forcing them offline.
Abusing domain replication rights to pull password hashes (including krbtgt) as if a domain controller.
Forged Kerberos TGT using the krbtgt hash: persistent, nearly undetectable domain dominance.
Security Operations Center: the team triaging alerts, hunting threats, and running incident response.
Security Information and Event Management: centralized log collection, correlation, and alerting (e.g., Sentinel).
Security Orchestration, Automation and Response: playbooks that automate triage and containment actions.
Endpoint Detection and Response: sensors on hosts recording process/file/network activity with automated response.
Proactive searching for undetected compromise using hypotheses (often ATT&CK-mapped), not waiting for alerts.
Indicator of Compromise: artifact of malicious activity (hash, IP, domain) used for detection and blocking.
Tactics, Techniques, Procedures: the behavioral patterns of adversaries (ATT&CK's organizing unit).
The public knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques, from Reconnaissance to Impact.
Kusto Query Language: the query language for Sentinel/Log Analytics — filter, summarize, join security data.
Structured analysis of what can go wrong (STRIDE), where trust boundaries lie, and which risks to mitigate.
How far a compromise can spread from one foothold; segmentation and least privilege shrink it.
Working at the customer boundary: shipping secure systems where the customer's risk actually lives.
Microsoft's Security Operations Analyst certification: Sentinel, Defender XDR, KQL, incident response.

faq.a: Learning is legal; *unauthorized access* is not. The course restricts practice to legal targets: your own labs, HackTheBox/TryHackMe, and contracted engagements with written scope. 'I was just testing' is not a defense.

faq.q: SOC analyst vs pentester — which path?
faq.a: SOC builds detection/response discipline and hires more juniors; pentesting needs deeper systems knowledge and usually comes later. The course covers both so you can choose with evidence.

faq.q: Do I need to memorize all of ATT&CK?
faq.a: No — memorize the 14 tactics and the 20 highest-frequency techniques; look up the rest. Interviewers test whether you can *map* an observed behavior to a technique, not recite IDs.

faq.q: How much KQL do I really need for SC-200?
faq.a: Working fluency: where/project/summarize/join/render, time charts, and joining SecurityAlert to device/process tables. The Sentinel module drills exactly this.
The course's offensive-practice spine: Linux and networking learned from the attacker's perspective on legal targets, progressing to full pentest methodology.

faq.q: How is this different from IL-11 (Zero Trust & Endpoint Defense)?
faq.a: IL-06 is the offensive+SOC operator track (pentest, hunting, Sentinel). IL-11 is the defender's Zero Trust architecture track (NIST 800-207, allowlisting, Entra ID, SC-300). They complement; IL-06 is the attack-informed half.

faq.q: Will this prepare me for Security+ too?
faq.a: Largely yes on concepts, but Security+ (SY0-701) has its own domain weights and terminology. IL-09 maps the CompTIA security track explicitly — use it alongside.
Borrowed from the Palantir-style model: engineers embedded at the customer boundary, shipping secure systems where the customer's risk lives rather than from a distant SOC.

tips: Follow the guided path in order — each module unlocks the next. The sequence is the curriculum; skipping ahead breaks the chain.

This course maps to CompTIA Security+ (SY0-701) and CompTIA CySA+ (CS0-003) (independent preparation — no affiliation). Weight your drill time toward the heaviest exam domains shown in the cert gates.
The math modules (Number Theory & Modular Arithmetic, Logic & Boolean Algebra, Probability & Statistics) are load-bearing — finish them before the applied modules that assume them.
Quiz-gated modules need 70%+ to unlock the next. When you miss a question, ask Noah to walk you through the miss Socratically before re-attempting.
Do each hands-on lab twice — once following the guide, once from a blank screen. The second pass is where the skill sticks.
This is a 46-hour course: about 12 hours a week finishes it in a month. Short daily sessions beat weekend cramming.

freshSignals.headline: NSA releases zero-trust guidance for hardening OT environments
freshSignals.brief: NSA's October 8 Cybersecurity Information Sheet translates zero trust into 26 high-impact activities for legacy operational technology — organized into ten mitigation steps from remote-access hardening to AD/domain-controller hardening. Key insight for defenders: most OT devices can't support modern auth or be patched without disrupting operations, so NSA recommends wrapping legacy assets in external compensating controls. The CSI also warns adversaries are using advanced AI to automate reconnaissance and accelerate exploit development.

freshSignals.headline: Citrix NetScaler hit by third zero-day in ten days (CVE-2026-88779)
freshSignals.brief: CVE-2026-88779 is a memory-overflow zero-day in the NetScaler ADC/Gateway SAML parser (CVSS 4.0 score 8.7), under active exploitation — the third actively exploited NetScaler zero-day in about ten days, after two RCEs (CVSS 9.5). CISA ordered federal agencies to patch by October 7. Edge appliances that terminate authentication are high-value targets: one crafted request can crash the service, and repeated requests keep it offline. This is exactly the 'assume breach, verify continuously' scenario zero-trust architecture is built for.
freshSignals.noahPrompt: Ask Noah: why are edge ADC/gateway appliances such attractive targets, and what does defense-in-depth look like when the edge itself is compromised?

freshSignals.headline: IBM Guardium's 11 CVEs: when the data-protection product needs protection
freshSignals.brief: IBM Guardium — a product literally built to protect data — picked up eleven CVEs this week, including three separate unauthenticated paths into the same product: an access-control bypass, a deserialization bug leading to code execution, and a listener on TCP port 16017 reachable by anyone who could reach it. The pattern: 'if you can reach it.' When a service has no network presence until a verified identity is authenticated, there is no allowlist to bypass and no port to find. Reachability decides how much is at stake while the patch is pending.
freshSignals.noahPrompt: Ask Noah to explain the 'reachability' argument: how does removing network presence change the economics of exploitation?

freshSignals.headline: Anthropic merges Cyber Verification Program with Project Glasswing
freshSignals.brief: Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program merged with Project Glasswing: 5,500+ verified vulnerabilities found April–October, with partners triaging 129K+ (33K+ critical/high). The expanded program gives vetted security professionals access to the latest Claude models for defensive work — a concrete example of frontier labs putting models in defenders' hands first (Google is doing the same with Gemini 4 Argon for vetted cyber defenders). For IL-31 learners: this is the institutional version of the red-team/blue-team loop.
freshSignals.noahPrompt: Ask Noah: how would you structure a responsible disclosure workflow that uses AI assistance without leaking the vulnerability?

freshSignals.headline: Gemini 4 Argon goes to vetted cyber defenders first
freshSignals.brief: Google is releasing Gemini 4 Argon to vetted cyber defenders first while US government pre-release evaluations run — part of the week's clear pattern of frontier capabilities being gated, withheld, or handed to defenders before general availability (OpenAI shelved GPT-6.1 Astra for not meeting authorization bar). For security learners, the takeaway: the most capable models are increasingly dual-use assets with controlled distribution, and 'vetted defender' programs are becoming a real access tier.
